title: Core Drawing Skills 2A — Structure & Observation
styleRules: Drawing itself stays monochrome graphite or neutral ink; G-Art pastel appears only in headings, arrows, small labels and framing accents.
Poster layout is chosen for the subject; do not force every lesson into the same five-column template.
Use one clearly defined transferable skill per poster.
All human examples receive an explicit final anatomy check at full resolution.
qaPrompts: balanced / symmetrical face appropriate to viewpoint
clear full-length shot or medium shot when the body is part of the lesson

items.title: Draw an Eye from Structure
items.learningGoal: Understand the eyeball, eyelid wrap, iris/pupil placement and simple light/shadow before adding lashes or style.
academicBasis: Foothill ART 4E: head/feature anatomy, proportions and light/shadow
Johns Hopkins portrait course: skull/feature structure and geometric simplification
items.suggestedLayout: One large construction sequence plus a bottom strip comparing front, 3/4 and side/turned eye views.
steps: Place a sphere/eye socket guide and the eye axis.
Wrap upper and lower lids around the sphere; avoid a flat almond symbol.
Place iris and pupil with correct occlusion by the upper lid.
Add one light source, lid shadow and a restrained highlight.
Refine lashes and surrounding planes only after structure reads.
visualChecks: both eyes align to head angle if shown on a face
iris remains circular in perspective, appearing elliptical when turned

items.title: Draw Hands from Simple Forms
items.learningGoal: Construct a readable hand from palm block, thumb base and finger groups, then refine joints and gesture.
academicBasis: Stanford Art and Anatomy: internal/external hand structure and observation
Foothill ART 4E: hand anatomy, proportions, planes, views and light
items.suggestedLayout: Large hand construction on left; three smaller practical poses on right; dedicated five-finger checklist box.
steps: Block the palm as a tapered box and mark wrist direction.
Attach the thumb base as a separate wedge with its own joint direction.
Group four fingers first, then separate them by length and joint rhythm.
Add knuckles, taper and overlap from observation.
Refine contour and simple shadow while preserving exactly five digits.
visualChecks: exactly five digits including one thumb whenever all fingers are visible
thumb originates from correct side of palm
small secondary hands receive the same inspection as the hero hand

items.title: Draw Hair as Masses, Then Strands
items.learningGoal: See hair as volume attached to a head, organized into flow groups, instead of drawing isolated strands from the start.
academicBasis: Observational drawing: contour/form relationships from UCSD and Foothill fundamentals
Portrait structure: head volume/viewpoint from Johns Hopkins
items.suggestedLayout: One head in 4 stages plus a variation row for straight, wavy and tied hair using different models.
steps: Establish skull volume and hairline before the hairstyle.
Draw the overall hair silhouette with clear space around the head.
Divide the hairstyle into a few large flow groups.
Show overlap and direction with selected interior lines.
Add only a small number of fine strands where they clarify texture or movement.
visualChecks: hair sits outside skull rather than replacing it
different examples use visibly different characters

items.title: Draw Fabric from Tension & Gravity
items.learningGoal: Understand why folds appear by locating support/tension points, gravity direction, compression and movement.
academicBasis: Foothill/UCSD drawing fundamentals: form, observation, light and contour
General studio principle: structure and forces before decorative fold lines
items.suggestedLayout: Four mini studies organized by cause: hanging, stretched, compressed and moving fabric; one final clothed figure crop.
steps: Find where the cloth is supported or pulled.
Mark the main direction of gravity or movement.
Group the largest folds before small wrinkles.
Separate stretched areas from compressed bunching.
Use value and edge changes to show thickness and overlap.
visualChecks: folds emerge from believable anchor/tension points
hands/arms under sleeves remain anatomically coherent when visible
